<reason>Both sides were disciplined, citation-free, and format-compliant, making this a tight technical debate over the motion's meaning. B's central "shrinkage" narrative — that PRO's exit right collapsed into CON's recalibration program — was rhetorically excellent but rests on a misreading: PRO's opening already defined the right as refusing the contaminated metric while being judged by checkable alternatives, not as unilateral immunity. Meanwhile B conceded the core outcome ("she keeps her job on the cleaned record"), leaving only the rights-versus-favor distinction, which A exploited effectively. B's two-tier/invisibility harm was blunted when A turned B's own metric list (telemetry, safety-carved completion rates, substantiated complaints) into evidence that unrated workers remain visible. A's systematic-bias point — averaging stabilizes rather than dilutes prejudice — was never fully neutralized; B's reply that human reviewers inherit the same bias with smaller samples was clever but thin. Both sides answered pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 structure; A's Q1 trap forced B's outcome-conceding answer. B's literal-text argument keeps the case competitive, but A made the decisive clash clearer and forced the more damaging concessions.</best_rebuttal>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's pressure Q2 forced Side B to list non-punishing metrics (B4.3), which A then weaponized in closing (A5.4) to dismantle the two-tier market argument — showing B's own "repaired thermometer" judges workers by exactly A's proposed alternatives, making exit from ratings no shield for bad actors.</best_rebuttal>
